content: CDCP1, also known as CUB domain-containing protein 1, is a protein encoded by the CDCP1 gene in humans. It is also referred to as CD318 (Cluster of Differentiation 318) and Trask (Transmembrane and associated with src kinases). Alternative splicing of the CDCP1 gene results in the production of distinct isoforms. CDCP1/Trask is not essential for the development of mice. Adult mice lacking CDCP1 do not display any significant morphological, reproductive, or behavioral abnormalities when compared to wild-type mice. Histological examinations of various organ systems in these mice have not revealed any notable pathological changes or differences in tissue structure. CDCP1 serves as a ligand for CD6, a receptor molecule expressed on certain T-cells. This interaction may influence T-cell migration and chemotaxis. Consequently, CDCP1 may play a role in the pathogenesis of autoimmune diseases such as encephalomyelitis, multiple sclerosis, and inflammatory arthritis. CDCP1 is a 140 kDa transmembrane glycoprotein characterized by a large extracellular domain (ECD) containing two CUB domains and a smaller intracellular domain (ICD). The extracellular domain of CDCP1 can be cleaved by serine proteases at a specific site adjacent to Arg368, resulting in a truncated 80 kDa protein. The relative expression levels of the full-length (p140) and truncated (p80) forms of CDCP1 vary among different cell lines, depending on the activity of endogenous serine proteases. Under normal physiological conditions, CDCP1 is not cleaved in vivo; however, cleavage can be induced during tumorigenesis or tissue injury. The intracellular domain of CDCP1 contains five tyrosine residues: Y707, Y734, Y743, Y762, and Y806. Phosphorylation of CDCP1 is exclusively mediated by Src kinases and is dependent on the adhesion state of the cells. In cultured cells, tyrosine phosphorylation of CDCP1 occurs when cells are induced to detach using trypsin or EDTA, or spontaneously during mitotic detachment. Loss of anchorage or cellular detachment is associated with CDCP1 phosphorylation and concurrent dephosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins, consistent with the disassembly of focal adhesions. Conversely, during cellular attachment, CDCP1 is dephosphorylated, which permits the phosphorylation of focal adhesion proteins. The anti-adhesion and anti-migratory functions of CDCP1 are mediated through its negative regulation of integrin receptors. Clinically, CDCP1 phosphorylation is observed in various cancers, including some pre-invasive cancers, invasive tumors, and metastatic lesions.
